title: Camfranglais
subtitle: From everyday language to transparent compiler decisions.
points: Product walkthrough, source-file guide and technical reference
notes: Introduce Camfranglais as the group's deterministic lexical and syntactic analyzer. This is a 100-slide reference presentation, not a claim that all 100 slides fit into the ten-minute oral assessment. Slide 99 provides a suggested short route. Screenshots show the real deployed application; no tests were created to capture them.

title: The group behind the project
subtitle: Three members. One shared compiler workspace.
notes: These are the known names and matricules already used in the documentation. No individual contribution assignments are invented. Instructor: Engr. Tanwi Nkiamboh. The group should review who presents each part before the assessment.

title: Three questions this deck answers
subtitle: Start with the experience. Follow the data. Find the implementation.
points: What can a visitor do on each of the five pages?
How does a statement become tokens, verdicts and a saved result?
Which real source file owns each part of that behavior?
notes: Use the small source rail on each slide to find the responsible files. Detailed paths and contextual explanations are also retained in the speaker notes. The presentation moves from the user interface to the algorithms and then to persistence, deployment and evidence.

title: Mixed language. Traceable rules.
subtitle: A teaching tool for inspecting informal urban communication.
points: French, English, Camfranglais and Pidgin evidence can coexist.
Keep spelling, apostrophes and punctuation visible.
Explain categories and grammar, not a translation.
notes: The illustration is original explanatory artwork, not a photograph or evidence of field collection. The application recognizes categories and language clues through rules and reference vocabulary. It is not an AI translator and does not infer a speaker's intent.

title: Five pages, one connected workflow
subtitle: Click a page card in the slideshow to jump to its walkthrough.
points: Enter text and record a test.
Browse supplied records, context and audio.
notes: App.tsx owns the public page list and hash navigation. The five public routes are compiler, analysis, collection, dictionary and examples. There are no public account, translator, imports or coursework-generation screens.

title: From statement to saved evidence
subtitle: The main journey has five visible outcomes.
notes: This is a simplified explanatory flow, not UML sequence notation. The detailed implementation validates the request and shared grammar before computation and persistence. Analyze in the current UI records an immutable public test, even when the parser rejects it.

title: Two verdicts. Different questions.
subtitle: A familiar word sequence is not automatically a grammatical match.
points:
Are any tokens UNKNOWN?
No unknowns means vocabulary approval.

Does the category sequence fit the saved CFG?
Known words can still reject.
notes: Vocabulary approval is based on UNKNOWN occurrences. Recognized slang, AMBIGUOUS and other known categories can pass it. CFG acceptance comes from predictive parsing. Neither result proves standard French correctness, meaning or authentic fieldwork.

title: Public does not mean editable
subtitle: The permission boundary is deliberate.
rows: Allowed when a matching file exists
Use accounts or private maintenance APIs
notes: The public session advertises analyze and save_tests capabilities while disabling reference edits. These restrictions are enforced in the backend, not merely by hiding buttons. CSRF protection remains even though login was removed.

title: Every feature has a source
subtitle: Read the source rail as a map, not just a list of filenames.
points: Chooses the page and connects navigation.
notes: The actual code is mostly Python functions and React function components. Do not rename these as imaginary controller or service classes. Paths on the slides are repository-relative; the complete repository accompanies the presentation.

title: The project at a glance
subtitle: Different numbers describe different parts of the system.
notes: The twelve statements are the fixed evaluation corpus. The 938 dictionary entries and 26 synthetic examples are not additional collected statements. The Collection snapshot contains those twelve sentences plus one approved Word annotation, choa.

subtitle: No account gate stands between the visitor and the input.

The public interface uses the operator-saved grammar.
The interface explains that tests become public.
notes: This screenshot is a real deployed page captured on 27 September 2026. The input is empty because the screenshot process did not submit a new test. The real input screen permits an empty-input grammar check.

title: Keep the speaker's original text
subtitle: The input is evidence, not text to silently repair.
points: The UI bounds one analyzer request.
A test is not added to Collection.
notes: The visual is a documented crop of the real input panel. Normalization is used later for matching and statistics; it does not replace the stored source text. An intentionally empty request is valid input to the analyzer flow, although the saved corpus grammar rejects it.

title: What happens after Analyze?
subtitle: A click starts a reproducible, server-side workflow.
notes: The endpoint used by the UI is POST /api/analyzer/tests. The request identifier supports safe retry. The public boundary and request models validate the operation before a result is saved. A grammar rejection is still a legitimate recorded result, not a failed network operation.

title: The client sends a reproducible request
subtitle: Three fields connect the UI to a specific computation.
points: The original string, not a translation.
The saved rule text used for this test.
Identical retry can find the same result.
notes: Angle-bracket values are explicitly abbreviated teaching placeholders, not a payload to copy unchanged. The actual request includes a valid UUID and full saved grammar. No CSRF token or private configuration is displayed in this example.

title: Waiting, stopping and retrying
subtitle: Browser state and server completion are not the same thing.
points: The analyzer allows up to 60 seconds for its request.
Abort the local wait, not a guaranteed server rollback.
Keep the request ID to recover the already-saved result.
notes: The general API helper has a shorter default timeout; the analyzer overrides it to 60000 ms. If the browser stops waiting, the server may still commit. Repeated completed tests with deliberately new request IDs count separately.

title: A test is an immutable snapshot
subtitle: Opening an old result does not run today's rules again.
points: The grammar used at that time.
A stable test ID and recorded time.
notes: Saved tests have no public edit or delete operation. An operator's later grammar or reference update does not rewrite prior lexical and syntactic results. This distinction is important when interpreting dashboard statistics.

title: An accepted example, token by token
subtitle: S02: je suis kass je go nang
notes: This slide is generated from the committed computed evidence, not typed token labels. The categories are FRENCH_FUNCTION_WORD, VERB, ADJECTIVE, FRENCH_FUNCTION_WORD, VERB, VERB. FF is used visually as an abbreviation for FRENCH_FUNCTION_WORD.

title: Rejection keeps the evidence
subtitle: The two unresolved corpus forms are not erased or repaired.
points:
The sixth token is UNKNOWN.
Five tokens are consumed before rejection.

The sixth token is UNKNOWN.
Later tokens are not silently skipped.
notes: Both original strings remain unchanged. Each rejected trace contains fourteen recorded rows. The parser reports the undefined table entry instead of treating UNKNOWN as a wildcard. Human review is needed to resolve the linguistic forms.

title: Reference, then draft, then explicit Analyze
subtitle: Opening a library item does not secretly create a test.
points: Copy its text to Franc Analyzer
Inspect the draft and retention notice
Explicitly run and save the test
notes: App.tsx coordinates the openCompiler handoff. It supplies a draft rather than automatically invoking the backend. This lets visitors inspect a source before choosing to publicly retain an analysis.

title: Analyzer: the files to open
subtitle: Use this map when explaining or debugging the main workflow.
points: Input, saved grammar, submit, retry and selected test.
JSON requests, CSRF headers and error messages.
Record, retrieve and report saved tests.
notes: Follow the UI event into the API file, then the route and history service. The compiler algorithms are intentionally separate from request orchestration and storage. The next chapter explains the evidence rendered from these saved results.

title: Analysis is the evidence desk
subtitle: Statistics and original results from publicly saved tests.
points: Inspect the original tokens and trace.
notes: The screenshot was captured from the live deployed application. Its totals describe the retained history at capture time, not the fixed twelve-statement evaluation. The two sets of numbers must not be merged.

title: Count saved tests, not collected records
subtitle: A dated history snapshot is different from a controlled study.
points: Token occurrences in the fixed study
notes: The first two values are observed on 27 September 2026 and can change as visitors submit new tests. The last two are fixed by the committed study. Untested Collection entries do not enter saved-test statistics.

title: Vocabulary approval asks one question
subtitle: Does the saved token stream contain UNKNOWN?
points:
Vocabulary ACCEPT.
Slang and AMBIGUOUS are not automatically rejected.

Vocabulary REJECT.
Keep the unresolved forms visible for review.
notes: The approval condition is exact: reject when unknown_count is positive. Empty input has no UNKNOWN tokens, so it passes this lexical condition even though the saved corpus grammar cannot derive an empty utterance.

title: Known words may still fail the CFG
subtitle: Constructed control: je je suis
points:
All three words have recognized categories.
Vocabulary approval passes.

The category order is unsupported.
The saved grammar rejects it.
notes: This is control C06, not an additional collected utterance. It demonstrates why separate verdicts matter. A dictionary-membership test alone could not explain this rejection.

title: Nine categories occur in the study
subtitle: Counts are generated from all 81 token occurrences.
points: Do not infer category coverage from the grammar alone.
notes: The lexer supports twenty terminal categories, but only nine occur in the twelve supplied statements. The chart is generated from statistics.category_counts. FF and EF abbreviate French and English function-word categories.

title: Frequency starts with actual tokens
subtitle: Most frequent forms in the controlled twelve-statement study.
points: These counts do not estimate language-wide usage.
notes: The bars use the first six entries of the computed frequency list. The corpus has 55 case-folded forms. Preserve the distinction between token occurrences and distinct forms, and avoid treating this small convenience corpus as representative of a whole population.

title: Inspect raw text and categories
subtitle: The selected-test panel makes individual decisions visible.
points: Compare each spelling with its chosen label.
This is a saved snapshot, not a new computation.
notes: This image comes from the genuine selected-S02 capture used in the report. The capture register preserves its original and cropped derivatives. It was opened read-only without submitting a test.

title: A trace is a sequence of decisions
subtitle: Each row records the stack and remaining input before its action.
points: Stack state / remaining categories / selected action.
notes: The displayed rows are the first four S02 trace records from computed evidence. In visual abbreviations: Ut is Utterance, Uf is Utterance_LF1, Cl is Clause, St is SubjectTail, and FF is FRENCH_FUNCTION_WORD. The full names are retained in the underlying evidence.

title: Grammar panels reveal the calculation
subtitle: The UI exposes intermediate results instead of only a green badge.
notes: GrammarResults renders the original and transformed grammar, transformation steps, sets and table. Conflicting entries are reported explicitly. These panels are read-only in the public workflow.

title: Analysis: rendering versus aggregation
subtitle: Different files own the view, the evidence and the totals.
points: Page wrapper, selected test and loading states.
Token tables, grammar tables and parse traces.
Aggregate saved snapshots and page summaries.
notes: Statistics are computed across saved tests even when only one summary page is returned. Pagination limits the displayed summaries, not the overall totals. Old snapshots are not silently reclassified.

title: Collection preserves supplied evidence
subtitle: A read-only browser for statements, annotations and context.
points: Open meanings, notes and available audio.
Copy a record into an analyzer draft.
notes: The current capture shows thirteen Collection entries: twelve sentences and one Word annotation. Review status is metadata, not proof of authentic original fieldwork. The public interface cannot create, edit or delete Collection records.

title: What one Collection record means
subtitle: Keep content, interpretation and provenance separate.
points: Location, review state and notes where present.
Playback or download when a stored file is available.
notes: EntryViewer presents these fields. A gloss is not an independently verified translation, and a recording does not alone establish who collected the original utterance or when. Missing metadata should remain missing rather than be filled with invented details.

title: Search and filter without rewriting
subtitle: Read-side tools help visitors find relevant records.
points: Filter language, review, category and type.
Download the filtered public result set.
Searching or exporting does not change a record.
notes: The screenshot is a crop of the real Collection page. Exported fields can include context and contributor details; the UI cautions users to share only with authorized recipients. The presentation capture did not export private data or mutate any record.

title: Twelve statements; provenance still qualified
subtitle: Software can measure the corpus without certifying its origin.
notes: The saved manual_transcription_confirmed flag is false and collection_method is blank. Some locations and audio references exist, but these do not prove collector identities, original dates, speakers or consent. This qualification remains explicit throughout the presentation.

title: Dictionary is a reference library
subtitle: Search vocabulary, supplied labels and source meanings.
points: Distinct reference entries, including retained senses.
See where a meaning or category came from.
Reference entries never increase research counts.
notes: The dictionary is assembled from the supplied classified CSV and retained Markdown sources. It is reference material, not the shared Collection. The UI separates source meanings and origins rather than inventing missing French translations.

title: Search kass and inspect its source
subtitle: A concrete lookup connects the interface to the reference data.
notes: This is a genuine current dictionary search, not a fabricated card. Opening the entry copies kass into the analyzer but does not run a test. The meaning and category are displayed as supplied source annotations, not independently validated linguistic facts.

title: Reference lookup does not overrule everything
subtitle: The classifier uses a defined priority order.
notes: The last card groups several later steps for a readable overview. classify_token checks French forms after the supplied reference and then morphological suffix heuristics. This is deterministic first-applicable-rule classification, not majority voting.

title: Synthetic means constructed, not collected
subtitle: Practice examples are useful precisely because they are labelled honestly.
points: Inspect topics, meanings and source labels.
Try a chosen example without altering Collection.
notes: Examples do not train the lexer or count as original field statements. They are explicitly constructed teaching material. Search and page navigation share the reference-search hook with the Dictionary.

title: Read-aloud reuses an existing recording
subtitle: There is no generated speech in the public workflow.
points: Stream existing bytes in the browser
notes: POST /api/readings/lookup is a read-only search, despite using POST. Upload, replace and delete are different write operations and are unavailable publicly. If there is no recording, the app must say so rather than synthesize a voice.

title: Library features: source ownership
subtitle: Three libraries share patterns, not the same evidence role.
notes: Collection search uses its own dataset-oriented controls. Dictionary and Examples reuse useReferenceSearch with a page size of 25 and a 250 ms debounce. Backend services keep source datasets separate.

title: Three working layers, one product
subtitle: The browser presents. The server coordinates. The compiler decides.
points: Pages, inputs, feedback and evidence panels.
Validation, public policy, endpoints and storage.
Regex lexing, grammar analysis and predictive parsing.
notes: Shared persistence supports the server layer. The explanatory illustration is original artwork, not a deployment proof. The current product is a lexical and syntactic analysis workspace; it does not emit machine code.

title: Boot without a login
subtitle: Public-session preparation replaces account authentication.
points: Render App and its five pages
notes: PublicSession rejects incompatible capabilities rather than silently assuming the backend is safe. The cookie and token provide request-origin protection. They are not a user account, fake identity or login session.

subtitle: Navigation stays inside the same application shell.
notes: All listed component files are under frontend/src. App.tsx chooses the route and handles shared navigation and focus. Unknown or retired fragments fall back to the analyzer rather than exposing removed screens.

subtitle: Two shared helpers keep page code focused.
points:
Owns pending and error state.
Prevents overlapping runs.
Supports cancel and clearError.

Sends JSON and CSRF headers.
Normalizes errors and timeouts.
Guards against stale sessions.
notes: These are hooks and functions, not classes. The default transport timeout is 15 seconds; the main analysis request explicitly uses 60 seconds. The UI must distinguish stop-waiting from durable cancellation.

subtitle: Production serves the compiled frontend and API together.
points: FastAPI serves JSON and static assets
notes: This is the documented deployment topology. Vite is a development and build tool, not the public production server. The presentation makes no new claim of audited VPS configuration or guaranteed uptime.

subtitle: The route reveals which part of the app is involved.
notes: Endpoint names are actual public interfaces. A POST is not automatically a write: recorded-reading lookup is an example of read-only POST. The analyzer test POST does persist a public result.

subtitle: The frontend verifies capabilities before opening the workspace.
points: No account or login is required.
notes: This is an abridged representation of the response contract. The real response also carries a CSRF token; no actual token is included on the slide. Capability validation is a frontend safeguard in addition to server-side enforcement.

title: Errors tell the user what happened
subtitle: A failed request is not a success-shaped empty result.
rows: Missing record or unavailable private API
Stale grammar or conflicting retry payload
notes: A valid grammar rejection is different from these transport and validation failures. It is a successful computation with accepted=false and a trace. This distinction prevents the UI from presenting server failures as linguistic conclusions.

title: The same workflow on a narrow screen
subtitle: Responsive presentation without changing the permission model.
points: Inputs and cards adapt to width.
notes: Both images are real 420-CSS-pixel viewport captures. Some mobile navigation is horizontally scrollable; the screenshot is not a complete list of all off-screen tabs. No special mobile write permissions exist.

title: Frontend file map: find the right layer
subtitle: Open the smallest responsible surface first.
notes: The lower source rail contains the core entry points, while the cards add the helper and evidence modules. All these files contain React/TypeScript functions except the explicit ApiError class inside api.ts.

title: Words become a typed token stream
subtitle: The lexer is the first algorithmic stage.
points: Recognize word forms, numbers and punctuation.
Assign a category using an ordered rule set.
Add language and phrase clues without deleting tokens.
notes: Token is a namedtuple with text and category. tokenize only segments; classify_token chooses labels; analyze_sentence assembles the lexical result. The rest of the compiler consumes the resulting categories.

title: Read the real segmentation branches
subtitle: TOKEN_SPLIT_RE preserves unsupported non-whitespace input.
code:
WORD:   letters + internal joiners
NUMBER: \d+(?:[.,]\d+)?
PUNCT:  [.,!?;:\"()]
OTHER:  \S

TOKEN_SPLIT_RE.findall(text)
points: Words, then numbers, punctuation and fallback.
An unsupported character survives for classification.
notes: The WORD line is a readable summary, not the complete source regex. Its exact Unicode and combining-mark definition appears in tokenizer.py. The other branches and findall call match the real code. The fallback prevents silently dropping unknown characters.

title: Internal joiners belong to the word
subtitle: Small boundary cases make the scanner behavior concrete.
rows: Dangling hyphen cannot finish a word
Repeated joiners break the word path
notes: These tokenization outputs were executed through the real tokenizer. Tokenization is not classification: the isolated hyphens subsequently become UNKNOWN. No original character is erased to make the example easier to parse.

title: Numbers are not signed literals
subtitle: The decimal branch requires digits on both sides of a separator.
notes: The lexer also permits comma as the decimal separator. The scanner does not recognize a signed-number syntax. These distinctions are included in the eight generated lexer controls that accompany the final report.

title: Unicode details change the boundary
subtitle: Not every apostrophe-like character takes the same transition.
points:
Pending joiners outside the word class.
Need a following word character.

Already belongs to Python's word-character class.
Follows the C edges, even at a boundary.
notes: C is [^\W\d_], not simply ASCII letters. Combining marks can continue a word according to the defined ranges. The DFA's joiner edge deliberately says outside C so the outgoing transitions remain deterministic.

title: Classification is ordered, not voted
subtitle: The first applicable rule determines the token category.
points: Slang, Pidgin, nouns, verbs and function words.
One category, or AMBIGUOUS for conflicting labels.
Observed French forms, then suffix heuristics.
notes: Within the explicit lists, the source order is slang, Pidgin, noun, verb, French function word, English function word. Approved annotations cannot displace the first structural number and punctuation checks. Suffix labels ending in _LIKE are heuristics, not confirmed parts of speech.

title: AMBIGUOUS is not UNKNOWN
subtitle: Preserve uncertainty instead of pretending all labels mean the same thing.
points:
The supplied reference has conflicting categories.
It is a known label, not a wildcard.

No supported classification matched.
It fails vocabulary approval.
notes: The saved corpus grammar allows AMBIGUOUS in specified positions only. It excludes UNKNOWN. Other explicitly authored grammars could include UNKNOWN as a terminal, but it would still not stand for an arbitrary category.

title: Normalize for matching. Preserve for evidence.
subtitle: A comparison key and the raw text serve different purposes.
notes: normalize_word uses lowercasing for ASCII and NFC/casefold plus apostrophe normalization otherwise. normalize_text also normalizes whitespace for comparisons. These functions are not a license to overwrite transcriptions.

title: Language clues and phrases are annotations
subtitle: Additional evidence must not collapse the token stream.
points: Sentence-ending punctuation resets the language run.
Preserve source-ordered raw spans as extra annotations.
notes: S02 includes the clue je ... go. Across the twelve statements there are 26 emitted transition clues, but zero matched verb phrases and zero matched slang phrases. Those zero results are evidence, not missing values to embellish.

title: Lexer files and responsibilities
subtitle: A small set of modules explains the complete lexical path.
notes: The module name learned does not imply machine learning. It derives a deterministic map from approved lexical annotations. Public visitors cannot edit those shared annotations through this app.

title: Grammar recognizes category sequences
subtitle: The parser reads labels, not the meaning of words.
points: A finite stream of lexer categories.
A context-free grammar of those categories.
Acceptance or an explicit failed transition.
notes: The saved category grammar is intentionally limited. It is not a complete grammar of Camfranglais. A sentence can match categories without being standard French, and meaningful language may fall outside the model.

title: The saved grammar is corpus-derived
subtitle: Reusable category structures, not a list of accepted sentences.
code:
Utterance -> Clause
           | Clause PUNCTUATION

Clause -> FRENCH_FUNCTION_WORD SubjectTail
        | Nominal BareSubjectTail
        | VERB PredicateTail
points: At most one optional punctuation token.
The two unresolved forms stay rejected.
notes: This is an excerpt of the actual original saved grammar. The full rationale in yaounde.py explains the observed structures and limitations. The saved snapshot is compared with this source by the evidence tests.

title: Starter grammar and saved grammar differ
subtitle: Do not confuse a fresh installation with the documented corpus state.
points:
DEFAULT_GRAMMAR in service.py.
Illustrative rules for an empty setup.

GRAMMAR in yaounde.py.
The group's saved category-level rules.
notes: The public analyzer loads the stored shared grammar. An empty data directory does not automatically reproduce the documented corpus and grammar. Only the generic starter has an immutable JSON analysis cache; custom grammars are analyzed afresh.

title: Read, transform, calculate, then parse
subtitle: Each phase produces inspectable output.
points: Remove supported recursion and factor prefixes
Run the category stream on the stack
notes: read_grammar raises GrammarError for invalid or oversized notation. transform_grammar records before/after snapshots. The table retains only unambiguous cells and reports conflicts separately. Predictive parsing is disabled for non-LL(1) grammars.

title: Remove the actual left recursion
subtitle: A noun cluster should not recurse before consuming input.
after:
Nominal -> NOUN Nominal_LR1
Nominal_LR1 -> NOUN Nominal_LR1 | epsilon
notes: This is an actual transformation from the corpus grammar, not a generic unrelated textbook example. The helper name is the one produced by the implementation. Epsilon is represented internally by an empty production list.

title: Factor the shared Clause prefix
subtitle: Choose the ending only after the common clause has been parsed.
after:
Utterance -> Clause Utterance_LF1
Utterance_LF1 -> epsilon | PUNCTUATION
points: The helper selects no ending or one punctuation token.
notes: This is the second actual grammar rewrite used in the report. The syntax layer records it as left_factor. It does not broaden the grammar to accept arbitrary repeated punctuation.

title: FIRST tells us what can start
subtitle: For the transformed study grammar:
notes: The three displayed categories are the computed FIRST set, not an assumption made from examples. calculate_first grows sets to a fixed point using first_of_sequence and nullable alternatives.

title: FOLLOW tells us what can come next
subtitle: End-of-input matters when a production is nullable.
points: Its FOLLOW set includes the end marker.
The LL(1) builder also uses FOLLOW lookaheads.
$ is a virtual marker, not a word typed by the visitor.
notes: calculate_follow scans productions in reverse while propagating trailers until stable. The dollar marker is appended logically to the category input. It is distinct from EPSILON, which denotes an empty derivation.

title: The study's transformed grammar
subtitle: Measured structure after the two recorded rewrites.
notes: The transformed grammar uses nine distinct terminal categories. These values are calculated from the committed saved grammar. They are not the number of supported categories in the lexer, which is twenty.

title: Syntax-analysis files: a map
subtitle: Locate notation, transformations, orchestration and execution.
points: Transform rules; compute sets and table.
notes: parse_tokens in service.py analyzes a grammar and delegates to parse_analysis. The latter can also consume a previously calculated grammar analysis without recalculation. These functions separate calculation from UI concerns.

title: Lexer DFA: recognizing token forms
subtitle: An equivalent formal model of the regex, not a runtime DFA class.
points: Unshown transitions stop this token path.
notes: W is word, I integer, F fraction, P punctuation and O another non-whitespace character. C is the Unicode word class excluding decimal digits and underscore; D is a decimal digit; M is a supported combining mark. Missing transitions enter an omitted dead state. This is formal automata notation, not UML state-machine notation.

title: A pending state cannot end a token
subtitle: Compare 3.14 with 3. using the same automaton.
points: With no following digit, emit 3 then scan . again
notes: For this particular regex, greedy matching retains the longest accepted prefix. A dangling joiner or separator is not included in a completed word or number. The remaining character is rescanned and preserved by another alternative.

title: The parser adds a stack
subtitle: Deterministic pushdown control explains the saved LL(1) recognizer.
points: Bottom marker and input end agree.
notes: The diagram uses buffered lookahead states q[a], one finite control state for each possible category or end marker. The implementation inspects categories[position] and advances only when matching. This is an equivalent recognition model, not a literal list of Python classes or a claim of unlimited memory.

title: The top of the stack is on the right
subtitle: S02 begins with a start symbol above the bottom marker.
points: Clause must be handled before the ending helper.
notes: The actual code initializes stack = [END, analysis['start_symbol']]. Popping the start symbol and extending with reversed(['Clause', 'Utterance_LF1']) leaves Clause at the rightmost top. The slide abbreviates long names only where the visual needs it.

title: One table entry controls expansion
subtitle: Nonterminal expansion does not consume a category.
points: Choose a unique M[A, a] entry.
Push the RHS in reverse order.
notes: The snippet is a focused excerpt with simplified table access and abbreviated trace text. The actual function checks that the row contains the lookahead and enforces the stack limit before applying the production. Conflicting table cells are never selected.

title: A terminal match consumes one category
subtitle: The stack and logical input advance together.
points: Record Match, pop, then increment position.
notes: This is the first terminal match in S02. FF abbreviates FRENCH_FUNCTION_WORD. Trace snapshots precede their actions, so the next trace row shows the changed stack and remaining input.

title: Walk the first four S02 actions
subtitle: Expansion and matching leave different fingerprints in the trace.
points: Only Match FF advances the remaining input.
notes: Explain each row while pointing at the rightmost stack item. The regression tests verify consecutive trace transitions, including reversed RHS pushes, non-consuming expansion and one-token matching. See slide 28 for the reading convention.

title: Acceptance and rejection are explicit
subtitle: Both outcomes return evidence rather than a guess.
points:
6 consumed tokens.
16 recorded trace rows.
Final stack and input both show $.

5 consumed tokens.
14 recorded trace rows.
UNKNOWN at the sixth token has no valid table entry.
notes: The accept path retains the bottom marker; it does not require an empty stack. A rejection includes an error and trace. It is still a valid computational result that the public app can store.

title: Bounds protect the parser
subtitle: The formal pushdown model is implemented with explicit resource limits.
notes: The parser also rejects malformed token structures, unsupported categories, conflicts, unresolved left recursion and repeated stack/input configurations. The 4,000-character analyzer request bound is a separate UI/API limit.

title: Four authored compiler classes, many functions
subtitle: Model the actual implementation, not invented service objects.
points: Token: namedtuple with text and category.
notes: The class diagram in the SDD verifies these four authored compiler runtime classes. Lexer, Parser and Grammar service classes are not invented. Grammar itself is a dictionary type alias and the main algorithms are module functions.

title: Shared storage is not an account
subtitle: One protected workspace supports all public visitors.
points: workspace.sqlite3 holds shared records and test snapshots.
notes: The active public database is under data_dir/shared-workspace. A stable internal public actor supports identifiers and idempotency, but it is not a fabricated user account. Public responses redact legacy ownership.

title: Save once, retry safely
subtitle: The snapshot and request mapping commit together.
notes: save_analyzer_request uses a BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction for analyzer_tests and test_requests. Repeating the same request ID with the same payload returns the existing test. Reusing it with a different payload causes a conflict.

title: Same retry versus a new stale request
subtitle: Grammar changes must not destroy the meaning of idempotency.
points:
Can return its original snapshot after an offline grammar change.
It is not a new computation.

A new request with outdated grammar returns 409.
Refresh the shared grammar before trying again.
notes: This subtle distinction preserves recoverability when the first response was lost. An identical retry is allowed to find its previous result. It does not authorize arbitrary new tests against a stale or editable browser grammar.

title: What is stored in a test?
subtitle: The saved evidence is enough to explain its original result.
points: The exact input and chosen rule snapshot.
Raw tokens, categories, counts and clues.
Accepted flag, consumed count, error and trace.
Stable ID, recorded time and contextual summaries.
notes: RecordedTest and related models validate internal consistency, including the relationship between tokens, parser consumption and vocabulary approval. Public snapshots are not replaced just because reference data later changes.

title: Web SQLite and desktop CSV are different
subtitle: Avoid explaining the active public store with the wrong persistence helper.
points:
SharedWorkspaceStore / WorkspaceStore.
